claim: Rotaviruses are a leading cause of severe diarrhea in young children and many mammalian species.
source: Rotaviruses (RVs), a leading cause of severe diarrhea in young children and many mammalian species, have evolved multiple strategies to counteract the host innate immunity
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about rotaviruses.

claim: Rotaviruses have evolved multiple strategies to counteract host innate immunity, specifically interferon (IFN) signaling through RV non-structural protein 1 (NSP1).
source: Rotaviruses (RVs), a leading cause of severe diarrhea in young children and many mammalian species, have evolved multiple strategies to counteract the host innate immunity, specifically interferon (IFN) signaling through RV non-structural protein 1 (NSP1).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: MAVS is critical for the host RNA sensing pathway upstream of IFN induction.
source: Here, we found that MAVS, critical for the host RNA sensing pathway upstream of IFN induction, is degraded by the RV RNA methyl- and guanylyl-transferase (VP3) in a host-range-restricted manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by established knowledge about MAVS function.

claim: MAVS is degraded by the RV RNA methyl- and guanylyl-transferase (VP3) in a host-range-restricted manner.
source: Here, we found that MAVS, critical for the host RNA sensing pathway upstream of IFN induction, is degraded by the RV RNA methyl- and guanylyl-transferase (VP3) in a host-range-restricted manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with experimental data.

claim: VP3 localizes to the mitochondria.
source: Mechanistically, VP3 localizes to the mitochondria and mediates the phosphorylation of a previously unidentified SPLTSS motif within the MAVS proline-rich region
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: VP3 mediates the phosphorylation of a previously unidentified SPLTSS motif within the MAVS proline-rich region.
source: Mechanistically, VP3 localizes to the mitochondria and mediates the phosphorylation of a previously unidentified SPLTSS motif within the MAVS proline-rich region
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: VP3-mediated phosphorylation of the SPLTSS motif leads to MAVS proteasomal degradation.
source: Mechanistically, VP3 localizes to the mitochondria and mediates the phosphorylation of a previously unidentified SPLTSS motif within the MAVS proline-rich region, leading to its proteasomal degradation
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by proteasome inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 2F and mutagenesis data in Figure 4G.

claim: VP3-mediated MAVS degradation leads to blockade of IFN-λ production in RV-infected intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Mechanistically, VP3 localizes to the mitochondria and mediates the phosphorylation of a previously unidentified SPLTSS motif within the MAVS proline-rich region, leading to its proteasomal degradation and blockade of IFN-λ production in RV-infected intestinal epithelial cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VP3 inhibition of MAVS activity contributes to enhanced RV replication in vivo.
source: Importantly, VP3 inhibition of MAVS activity contributes to enhanced RV replication and to viral pathogenesis in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo mouse infection data shown in Figure 5.

claim: VP3 inhibition of MAVS activity contributes to viral pathogenesis in vivo.
source: Importantly, VP3 inhibition of MAVS activity contributes to enhanced RV replication and to viral pathogenesis in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo mouse infection data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cytoplasmic RNA pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) generated during virus replication are sensed by host pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) including RIG-I and MDA5.
source: Cytoplasmic RNA pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) generated during virus replication, including viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) intermediate or genome, 5'-triphosphate RNA and other byproducts, are sensed by host pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) including RIG-I and MDA5 (Kato et al., 2006; Uzri and Greenberg, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PRRs activate the mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) for downstream signal transduction and IFN production.
source: PRRs in turn activate the mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS), a predominantly mitochondria and partially peroxisome-resident protein (Bender et al., 2015; Odendall et al., 2014), for downstream signal transduction and IFN production (Seth et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MAVS is a predominantly mitochondria and partially peroxisome-resident protein.
source: PRRs in turn activate the mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS), a predominantly mitochondria and partially peroxisome-resident protein (Bender et al., 2015; Odendall et al., 2014), for downstream signal transduction and IFN production (Seth et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mavs-/- mice are highly susceptible to multiple RNA virus infections, such as West Nile virus (WNV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3), rotavirus (RV), and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV).
source: Due to its central role in host antiviral immunity, Mavs-/- mice are highly susceptible to multiple RNA virus infections, such as West Nile virus (WNV) (Pinto et al., 2014), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) (Bhoj et al., 2008), coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) (Wang et al., 2010), rotavirus (RV) (Broquet et al., 2011), and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) (Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations for each virus.

claim: MAVS expression in the hematopoietic compartment is critical for proper T cell functions.
source: MAVS expression in the hematopoietic compartment is also critical for proper T cell functions (Zhao et al., 2016) and a T cell-independent antibody response (Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: MAVS expression in the hematopoietic compartment is critical for a T cell-independent antibody response.
source: MAVS expression in the hematopoietic compartment is also critical for proper T cell functions (Zhao et al., 2016) and a T cell-independent antibody response (Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Multiple virus-encoded factors inhibit MAVS signaling through its cleavage or degradation, including hepatitis C virus (HCV) NS3/4A protease, hepatitis A virus (HAV) 3ABC precursor, enterovirus (EV) 71 2Apro, and coronavirus SARS-CoV ORF9b.
source: Multiple virus-encoded factors, including hepatitis C virus (HCV) NS3/4A protease (Bender et al., 2015; Li et al., 2005; Ferreira et al., 2016), hepatitis A virus (HAV) 3ABC precursor (Yang et al., 2007), enterovirus (EV) 71 2Apro (Wang et al., 2013) and coronavirus SARS-CoV ORF9b (Shi et al., 2014), all inhibit MAVS signaling through its cleavage or degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations for each viral factor.

claim: The ability of HAV to block human but not murine MAVS constitutes the basis of the HAV relative host range restriction to humans in vivo.
source: In fact, the ability of HAV to block human but not murine MAVS constitutes the basis of the HAV relative host range restriction to humans in vivo (Hirai-Yuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The viral MAVS antagonists identified to date have been mostly non-structural proteins with the exception of influenza PB2.
source: Interestingly, the viral MAVS antagonists identified to date have been mostly non-structural proteins with the exception of influenza PB2 (Long and Fodor, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: RV VP3 possesses phosphodiesterase (PDE) activity.
source: In the present study, we report the unexpected discovery that the RV RNA capping enzyme VP3, an important RV structural protein, recently shown to also possess phosphodiesterase (PDE) activity (Zhang et al., 2013), also mediates MAVS degradation in an RV strain-specific manner.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: VP3 expression during RV infection induces specific degradation of the full-length functional MAVS protein but not the truncated 'mini'-MAVS that does not activate IFN signaling.
source: Additionally, VP3 expression during RV infection induces specific degradation of the full-length functional MAVS protein but not the truncated 'mini'-MAVS that does not activate IFN signaling (Brubaker et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 2B showing differential degradation of FL-MAVS vs mini-MAVS.

claim: Rotaviruses are segmented, dsRNA viruses that primarily infect the mature intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) located at the tip of the villi in the host small intestine.
source: RVs are segmented, dsRNA viruses that primarily infect the mature intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) located at the tip of the villi in the host small intestine (Estes and Greenberg, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A large number of mammalian and avian species are infected with their own host specific RV strains in a host range restricted fashion.
source: A large number of mammalian and avian species are infected with their own host specific RV strains in a host range restricted fashion (Ciarlet et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Both type I and type III IFNs are able to effectively restrict the replication of heterologous (non-murine) but not homologous (murine) RVs in suckling mice.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that both type I and type III IFNs are able to effectively restrict the replication of heterologous (non-murine) but not homologous (murine) RVs in suckling mice (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: In RV infected suckling mice, the bulk of type I IFNs (IFN-α/β) derive from the CD45+ hematopoietic compartment whereas type III IFNs (IFN-λs) are produced primarily by the intestinal epithelium.
source: It was also noted that in RV infected suckling mice, the bulk of type I IFNs (IFN-α/β) derive from the CD45+ hematopoietic compartment whereas type III IFNs (IFN-λs) are produced primarily by the intestinal epithelium (Lin et al., 2016; Sen et al., 2012; Hernández et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Wild-type HT-29 cells expressed and secreted significantly more IFNL3 mRNA (40–60 fold) and IFN-λ protein (31–34 fold) than type I IFN (IFNB) in response to poly(I:C) stimulation or RV infection.
source: We noted that wild-type (WT) HT-29 cells expressed and secreted significantly more IFNL3 mRNA (40–60 fold) and IFN-λ protein (31–34 fold) than type I IFN (IFNB) (Figure 1A), in response to RNA PAMPs, such as stimulation with poly(I:C), a dsRNA mimic, or RV infection
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MAVS-/- HT-29 cells were completely defective in both IFN-β and IFN-λ production in response to poly(I:C) or RV infection.
source: In contrast, MAVS-/- HT-29 cells were completely defective in both, suggesting that: (1) HT-29 cells produced more IFN-λ than IFN-β, and (2) that this IFN secretory process was mediated through the RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS RNA sensing pathway in HT-29 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Following infection with RV or vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), human IECs expressed much more (50 fold) IFNL3 than IFNB.
source: Consistent with the findings in HT-29 cells, we found that following infection with RV or vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), an excellent source of RNA PAMPs (Kell and Gale, 2015), human IECs expressed much more (50 fold) IFNL3 than IFNB (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both IFNB and IFNL3 expression were reduced to baseline levels in the absence of MAVS in HEK293 cells.
source: Both IFNB and IFNL3 expression were reduced to baseline levels in the absence of MAVS (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Human IECs intrinsically differ from some human non-intestinal origin cells and preferentially express IFN-λ over IFN-β in response to RNA PAMP stimulation.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that human IECs intrinsically differ from some human non-intestinal origin cells and preferentially express IFN-λ over IFN-β in response to RNA PAMP stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Replication of the simian RV RRV strain was enhanced approximately 10-fold in the absence of MAVS in HT-29 cells.
source: Interestingly, although replication of the simian RV RRV strain was enhanced approximately 10-fold in the absence of MAVS, the replication of the human RV Wa strain was not significantly increased (Figure 2A, top panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The replication of the human RV Wa strain was not significantly increased in the absence of MAVS in HT-29 cells.
source: Interestingly, although replication of the simian RV RRV strain was enhanced approximately 10-fold in the absence of MAVS, the replication of the human RV Wa strain was not significantly increased (Figure 2A, top panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The amount of infectious RRV, but not Wa RV, was markedly increased in the supernatant of MAVS-/- HT-29 cells compared to WT cells.
source: In addition to intracellular viral RNA levels, the amount of infectious RRV, but not Wa RV, was also markedly increased in the supernatant of MAVS-/- HT-29 cells compared to WT cells (Figure 2A, lower panel)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A significant decrease in the levels of FL-MAVS (by 6 hr) and IRF1 (by 12 hr) was observed in African Green Monkey MA104 cells following simian RRV infection.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the levels of FL-MAVS (by 6 hr) and IRF1 (by 12 hr) in African Green Monkey MA104 cells following simian RRV infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The FL-MAVS down-regulation during RRV infection was highly specific, as the levels of mini-MAVS and other signaling molecules were only affected at high MOI and late time points.
source: The FL-MAVS down-regulation was highly specific, as the levels of mini-MAVS, a truncated isoform that is unable to trigger IFN induction (Brubaker et al., 2014), other signaling molecules (RIG-I, TBK1, IKKε, TRAF2, β-TrCP), control mitochondrial (Fis1, COXIV), and peroxisomal (PMP70) proteins were only affected at a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 10 and only at the latest time point examined (12 hr post infection) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transcript levels of MAVS mRNA remained stable during RV infection.
source: Moreover, transcript levels of MAVS mRNA, from which both FL and mini-MAVS are translated (Brubaker et al., 2014), remained stable during RV infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RV infection induced FL-MAVS degradation in an RV strain-dependent manner.
source: Surprisingly, we also noted that RV infection induced FL-MAVS degradation in an RV strain-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only the simian RRV and, to a much lesser extent, the porcine SB1A strain, were able to induce MAVS degradation in rhesus origin MA104 cells.
source: Compared to several other animal and human RV strains, only the simian RRV and, to a much lesser extent, the porcine SB1A strain, were able to induce MAVS degradation in rhesus origin MA104 cells (Figure 2C, upper panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, middle panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Infection of human origin HT-29 cells with the human RV Wa strain, but not the simian RRV strain, was capable of degrading human MAVS.
source: In contrast, infection of the human origin HT-29 cells with the human RV Wa strain, but not the simian RRV strain, was capable of degrading human MAVS (Figure 2C, middle panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, lower panel)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only the murine RV ETD strain efficiently degraded murine MAVS in NIH3T3 cells.
source: These associations were further documented in NIH3T3 cells, a mouse origin fibroblast cell line, where only the murine RV ETD strain efficiently degraded murine MAVS (Figure 2C, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RRV infection diminished luciferase production driven by IFN and ISG promoters in MA104 cells in response to RNA PAMP stimulation.
source: As expected, we found diminished luciferase production driven by IFN and ISG promoters in RRV infected MA104 cells in response to ensuing RNA PAMP stimulation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Efficient MAVS degradation requires active RV replication and likely de novo synthesis of viral proteins.
source: However, efficient MAVS degradation requires active RV replication and likely de novo synthesis of viral proteins, as either psoralen UV-inactivation or neutralizing antibody pre-incubation prevented MAVS inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only proteasome inhibitors MG132, lactacystin and bortemozib, but not lysosome inhibitors, pan-caspase inhibitor, or mTOR inhibitor, rescued MAVS expression to WT levels during RV infection.
source: However, we found that among the nearly 50 drug compounds tested, only proteasome inhibitors MG132, lactacystin and bortemozib, but not lysosome inhibitors chloroquine and concanamycin A, pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK, or mTOR inhibitor rapamycin, rescued MAVS expression to WT levels (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: MAVS degradation during RV infection is likely mediated via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
source: However, we found that among the nearly 50 drug compounds tested, only proteasome inhibitors MG132, lactacystin and bortemozib, but not lysosome inhibitors chloroquine and concanamycin A, pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK, or mTOR inhibitor rapamycin, rescued MAVS expression to WT levels (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that MAVS degradation during RV infection is likely mediated via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Only the expression of RV VP3 and viroporin NSP4 could possibly lead to the degradation of endogenous FL-MAVS in MA104 cells.
source: The present data indicate that only the expression of RV RNA methyl- and guanylyl-transferase VP3 and viroporin NSP4 could possibly lead to the degradation of endogenous FL-MAVS in MA104 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a significant dose dependent reduction of ectopically expressed rhesus MAVS by simian RRV VP3 but not RRV NSP1.
source: These findings are further supported by the significant dose dependent reduction of ectopically expressed rhesus MAVS by simian RRV VP3 but not RRV NSP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only the two reassortant RVs that encoded an RRV VP3 (7-1-1 and 27-3-1) were able to degrade rhesus MAVS in MA104 cells.
source: Moreover, using a series of reassortant RVs derived from the simian RRV and bovine UK RV strains (Feng et al., 2011), we found that only the two reassortant RVs that encoded an RRV VP3 (7-1-1 and 27-3-1) were able to degrade rhesus MAVS in MA104 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, upper panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only the two reassortant RVs derived from the cross of simian RRV and murine EW RVs, both of which encoded a murine RV VP3 (B7/2 and D6/2), were able to degrade murine MAVS in NIH3T3 cells.
source: Similarly, only the two reassortant RVs derived from the cross of simian RRV and murine EW RVs, both of which encoded a murine RV VP3 (B7/2 and D6/2), were able to degrade murine MAVS in NIH3T3 cells as compared to WT RRV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, lower panel)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MAVS degradation is mediated by VP3, not NSP1.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly suggest that MAVS degradation is mediated by VP3, not NSP1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and biochemical data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only VP3 and not NSP3 or NSP4, was enriched in the immune-precipitate of the MG132 group in which MAVS proteasomal degradation was inhibited.
source: Notably, although the total levels of VP3 did not increase in MG132-treated cells (data not shown), only VP3 and not NSP3 or NSP4, was enriched in the immune-precipitate of the MG132 group in which MAVS proteasomal degradation was inhibited (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: VP3 physically interacts with MAVS.
source: We further interrogated possible VP3-MAVS interactions using traditional IP with both ectopic expression of Flag-tagged MAVS and GFP-tagged VP3 (Figure 3D) and purified recombinant MAVS and VP3 proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). While NSP4 did not co-precipitate with MAVS (Figure 3D), in both cases, we observed VP3 in the IP lysates, again suggesting that the VP3-MAVS, but not the NSP4-MAVS, interaction is likely to be direct.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A previously uncharacterized N-terminal region (171 amino acids) of VP3 was important for its mitochondrial localization.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that a previously uncharacterized N-terminal region (171 amino acids) of VP3 was important for its mitochondrial localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NSP1 was largely localized to the Golgi apparatus and did not co-localize with MAVS.
source: In contrast, NSP1 was largely localized to the Golgi apparatus as previously reported (Ding et al., 2016) and did not co-localize with MAVS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The N-terminal domain of VP3 was sufficient to induce MAVS degradation.
source: Importantly, the N-terminal domain itself, which turns out to be the most variable region with VP3 (Ogden et al., 2014), was sufficient to induce MAVS degradation (Figure 3E, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The N-terminal domain of VP3 is the MAVS-interacting part of VP3.
source: Co-IP experiments also pinpointed the N-terminal domain to be the MAVS-interacting part of VP3 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The C-terminal PDE domain of VP3 was not required for MAVS degradation.
source: We found that the C-terminal PDE domain, recently shown to prevent RNaseL activation (Zhang et al., 2013; Sánchez-Tacuba et al., 2015), was not required for MAVS degradation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Neither pharmacological inhibitors of PDE activity nor site-directed mutagenesis of the two key histidine residues (H718, H797) within the PDE catalytic sites rescued MAVS levels.
source: Importantly, neither pharmacological inhibitors of PDE activity nor site-directed mutagenesis of the two key histidine residues (H718, H797) within the PDE catalytic sites rescued MAVS levels (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The PDE enzymatic activity of VP3 was not involved in MAVS degradation.
source: Importantly, neither pharmacological inhibitors of PDE activity nor site-directed mutagenesis of the two key histidine residues (H718, H797) within the PDE catalytic sites rescued MAVS levels (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that unlike RNaseL inhibition (Zhang et al., 2013), the PDE enzymatic activity itself was not involved in MAVS degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There is a specific interaction between simian MAVS and VP3 from simian RV RRV strain, and not with VP3 from murine and human RV strains.
source: Consistent with our observation in the context of virus infections (Figure 2), we observed a specific interaction between simian MAVS and VP3 from simian RV RRV strain, and not with VP3 from murine and human RV strains (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Replacing the first 171 N-terminal amino acids from simian RRV strain with those from murine ETD RV strain completely abrogated the VP3-MAVS interaction.
source: Importantly, replacing the first 171 N-terminal amino acids from simian RRV strain with those from murine ETD RV strain completely abrogated the VP3-MAVS interaction (Figure 3H)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Blocking the proteasome by MG132 prevented MAVS degradation by VP3.
source: We also found that, similar to RV infection, blocking the proteasome by MG132 prevented MAVS degradation by VP3 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: RV structural protein VP3 localizes to the mitochondria and interacts with and targets MAVS for proteasomal degradation.
source: Nevertheless, our results clearly indicate that using its N-terminal region, RV structural protein VP3 localizes to the mitochondria and interacts with and targets MAVS for proteasomal degradation (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CARD-PRR alone is sufficient for MAVS-VP3 interaction.
source: Although CARD-PRR alone is sufficient for MAVS-VP3 interaction (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The levels of EGFP-TM and CARD-PRR-EGFP remained stable during RV infection.
source: Although CARD-PRR alone is sufficient for MAVS-VP3 interaction (Figure 4B), the levels of EGFP-TM and CARD-PRR-EGFP remained stable during RV infection (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CARD-PRR-EGFP-TM encoding both the first 200 amino acids and the C-terminal TM region was degraded at almost the same efficiency as FL-MAVS.
source: Conversely, CARD-PRR-EGFP-TM encoding both the first 200 amino acids and the C-terminal TM region was degraded at almost the same efficiency as FL-MAVS (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Multiple MAVS domains, in particular its mitochondrial localization, may be required for efficient degradation by RV VP3.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that while the CARD domain may be important for VP3 binding, multiple MAVS domains, in particular its mitochondrial localization, may be required for efficient degradation by RV VP3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Lysine 10 is more important in VP3-mediated MAVS degradation than lysine 7.
source: We found that lysine 10 is more important in VP3-mediated MAVS degradation, as mutation of K10 partially rescued MAVS levels in both single and double mutants K10A and K7AK10A respectively (Figure 4D, upper panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Changing lysines to arginines to conserve the positive charge (K7RK10R) partially blocked RV-infection induced MAVS degradation.
source: Changing lysines to arginines to conserve the positive charge (K7RK10R) also partially blocked RV-infection induced MAVS degradation (Figure 4D, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: K10 is highly conserved among MAVS from different species and is also required for its degradation by human RV infection.
source: K10 is highly conserved among MAVS from different species and is also required for its degradation by human RV infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: During RRV infection, MAVS was modified by K48 poly-ubiquitination.
source: Through the use of a panel of ubiquitin mutants, we noted that during RRV infection, MAVS was modified by K48 poly-ubiquitination (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: High-resolution IP-MS revealed three novel arginine methylation sites and a cluster of phosphorylated residues within MAVS that had not been previously reported.
source: Although we did not detect any glycosylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, upper panel) or AMPylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, lower panel), our high-resolution IP-MS using mock or RV-infected cell lysates and antibody against endogenous MAVS revealed three novel arginine methylation sites and a cluster of phosphorylated residues that had not been previously reported in phospho-proteome databases (Hornbeck et al., 2015) and thus represents novel phosphorylation hotspots (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The phosphorylation region consists of 188SPLTSS193 and is located in the proline-rich region (PRR) of MAVS.
source: Similar to the prior characterization of serine-rich clusters (Liu et al., 2015), this region consists of 188SPLTSS193 and is located in PRR, which we found to be required for VP3-mediated MAVS degradation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A and 4F.

claim: Within the SPLTSS motif, two serines and one threonine were phosphorylated during RV infection and these phosphorylation modifications were individual events that totaled to 16.0% of total MAVS proteins.
source: Within the SPLTSS motif, two serines and one threonine were phosphorylated during RV infection and these phosphorylation modifications were individual events that totaled to 16.0% of total MAVS proteins (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The same phosphorylation modifications in the SPLTSS motif were detected when recombinant VP3 was expressed alone.
source: We further detected the same phosphorylation modifications in the SPLTSS motif when recombinant VP3 was expressed alone (data not shown), further indicating that this process is entirely mediated by RV VP3.
evidence: This is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: Mutagenesis of the SPLTSS motif to six alanines completely abolished RV-induced MAVS degradation.
source: Remarkably, mutagenesis of the SPLTSS motif to six alanines completely abolished RV-induced MAVS degradation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Mutation of all three methylated arginines to alanines did not prevent MAVS degradation.
source: In contrast, mutation of all three methylated arginines to alanines did not prevent MAVS degradation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Disruption of the highly conserved SPLTSS motif in human MAVS prevented MAVS phosphorylation and inhibited human RV-induced degradation.
source: Importantly, disruption of this highly conserved SPLTSS motif in human MAVS also prevented MAVS phosphorylation and inhibited human RV-induced degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VP3 from human RV binds to human MAVS but not to simian MAVS.
source: As expected, we observed specific binding of VP3 from human RV to human MAVS but not to simian MAVS (Figure 4H)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Disruption of either the SPLTSS motif or the three-arginine site did not alter interaction with VP3.
source: Interestingly, disruption of either the SPLTSS motif or the three-arginine site did not alter interaction with VP3 (Figure 4H), implying that VP3-MAVS interaction occurs independent of the SPLTSS motif.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: MAVS proteins, including the SPLTSS and K7RK10R mutants, were still fully functional at inducing type I and type III IFN expression.
source: We also found that these MAVS proteins, including the SPLTSS and K7RK10R mutants, were still fully functional at inducing type I and type III IFN expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A pronounced decrease in the total protein levels of MAVS was observed in EW-infected IECs but not in IECs following RRV infection in vivo.
source: Consistent with our findings in cell culture, we observed a pronounced decrease in the total protein levels of MAVS in EW-infected IECs but not in IECs following RRV infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mavs transcripts within the sorted IECs remained stable during RV infection in vivo.
source: Mavs transcripts within the sorted IECs remained stable during RV infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), confirming that the decrease in MAVS occurred at a post-transcriptional level.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Despite significantly higher levels of virus replication, EW induced less IFN-λ expression than RRV in vivo.
source: Despite significantly higher levels of virus replication, EW induced less IFN-λ expression than RRV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The replication of RRV was significantly lower than EW in WT animals.
source: In WT animals, the replication of RRV was significantly lower than EW, consistent with our previous publications (Lin et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2013) and viral protein levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and citations.

claim: The amount of RRV shedding in the feces was markedly enhanced (1–2 logs) in Mavs-/- animals compared to WT littermates.
source: Remarkably, the amount of RRV shedding in the feces was markedly enhanced (1–2 logs) in Mavs-/- animals compared to WT littermates (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The fecal antigen levels of EW were not significantly different between WT and Mavs-/- animals.
source: In contrast, the fecal antigen levels of EW were not significantly different (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The viral RNA level of intra-intestinal simian RRV replication, but not murine EW RV replication, was increased in Mavs-/- mice.
source: The viral RNA level of intra-intestinal simian RRV replication, but not murine EW RV replication, was increased in Mavs-/- mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RRV replication at the liver increased by one log in the Mavs-/- pups at day 7 post infection.
source: RRV replication at certain extra-intestinal sites, such as the liver, also increased by one log in the Mavs-/- pups at day 7 post infection (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The intestinal and systemic replication of the murine EW RV was almost identical between WT and Mavs-/- groups.
source: In contrast, the intestinal and systemic replication of the murine EW RV was almost identical between the two groups (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: RRV replication in the small intestine was substantially up-regulated (approximately 100-fold) in Ifnar1-/-, Mavs-/-, Casp1-/- and Nlrp9b-/- mice but not in Il18-/- animals.
source: We found that the RRV replication in the small intestine was substantially up-regulated (approximately 100-fold) in Ifnar1-/-, Mavs-/-, Casp1-/- and Nlrp9b-/- mice but not in Il18-/- animals (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The suppressive effect on RV fecal shedding of Nlrp9b was much more profound for simian RV than that for the homologous murine RV.
source: It is worth noting that the suppressive effect on RV fecal shedding of Nlrp9b was much more profound for simian RV than that for the homologous murine RV (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: Simian RV replication is substantially restricted by both inflammasome and IFN signaling.
source: These findings suggest that, in contrast to murine RV replication, which is modestly controlled by the STAT1 signaling (Lin et al., 2016) and inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis (Zhu et al., 2017), 1) simian RV replication is substantially restricted by both inflammasome and IFN signaling
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data shown in Figure 5C and cited studies.

claim: Pyroptosis (cell death), but not inflammasome-mediated pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion (in particular IL-18), leads to both EW and RRV attenuation in vivo.
source: These findings suggest that, in contrast to murine RV replication, which is modestly controlled by the STAT1 signaling (Lin et al., 2016) and inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis (Zhu et al., 2017), 1) simian RV replication is substantially restricted by both inflammasome and IFN signaling, 2) pyroptosis (cell death), but not inflammasome-mediated pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion (in particular IL-18), leads to both EW and RRV attenuation in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pex-MAVS induces both IFN-λ and IFN-β expression.
source: However, we also found that despite the controversy in literature (Bender et al., 2015; Odendall et al., 2014), in our system pex-MAVS expression in a MAVS-depleted background strongly activated both type I and type III IFNs to a similar degree as WT MAVS and mito-MAVS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mini-MAVS was defective in IFN induction.
source: Through reconstitution of WT MAVS, mitochondria-only MAVS (mito-MAVS), peroxisome-only MAVS (pex-MAVS) and mini-MAVS, we found that, consistent with a previous study (Brubaker et al., 2014), mini-MAVS was defective in IFN induction.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.
